narrative:
The model predicted a 64% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your performance in the third year of law school had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the second decile, far below the average of roughly sixth-decile performance among students who were accepted. Your LSAT score was the second most important factor and also pulled the outcome toward failure; a score of 25 sits substantially below the 37-point average of admitted students. Family income worked in the opposite direction, modestly supporting a higher chance of passing, because you come from an upper-middle income background that is common among successful applicants.

Taken together, the model saw your lower academic standing in law school and modest LSAT performance as clear signals that the first-time bar passage risk was too high for admission.

What you should do next is focus on strengthening the areas the model weighed most heavily. Retake the LSAT and aim for a meaningfully higher score, while also working to raise your academic performance in the remaining law school years. These improvements would directly address the factors that led to the rejection and improve your chances in a future application. (218 words)
